theory.title: Theory
theory.description: Basic checkmates: two rooks, queen, rook.

twoRooksMate.title: Two-rook checkmate
twoRooksMate.description: The 'ladder' method — two rooks alternately push the opponent's king to the edge of the board. Also known as the linear mate.

queenMate.title: Queen checkmate
queenMate.description: King and queen versus a lone king. The queen restricts space; the king helps to deliver mate.

rookMate.title: Rook checkmate
rookMate.description: King and rook versus a lone king. King opposition plus a cutting line by the rook.

windmill.title: Windmill
windmill.description: Tactical pattern: a sequence of discovered checks by bishop and rook lets you pick off the opponent's pieces one by one.

steinitz.name: Wilhelm Steinitz
steinitz.description: First official World Chess Champion. Founder of the positional school, introduced the principles of accumulating small advantages.

lasker.name: Emanuel Lasker
lasker.description: World champion for 27 years — a record. Known for his psychological approach and universal style.

capablanca.name: José Raúl Capablanca
capablanca.description: Cuban genius with phenomenal intuition. Hardly lost a game during his prime.

alekhine.name: Alexander Alekhine
alekhine.description: Famous for aggressive style and deep combinations. The only champion to die while holding the title.

euwe.name: Max Euwe
euwe.description: Dutch champion and mathematician. Defeated Alekhine in their 1935 match.

botvinnik.name: Mikhail Botvinnik
botvinnik.description: Patriarch of the Soviet chess school. Mentored a whole generation of champions.

smyslov.name: Vasily Smyslov
smyslov.description: Known for his harmonious style and outstanding endgame technique.

tal.name: Mikhail Tal
tal.description: The 'Magician from Riga'. Legendary tactician famed for sacrifices and attacking play.

petrosian.name: Tigran Petrosian
petrosian.description: Master of defense and prophylaxis. One of the toughest players ever to crack.

spassky.name: Boris Spassky
spassky.description: All-rounder. World champion who lost the title to Fischer in 1972.

fischer.name: Bobby Fischer
fischer.description: Chess legend who broke Soviet dominance. World champion in 1972.

karpov.name: Anatoly Karpov
karpov.description: Master of positional play and control. Dominated the 1970s–80s.

kasparov.name: Garry Kasparov
kasparov.description: One of the strongest players in history. Aggressive style and deep opening preparation.

why.title: Why this project
why.p1: Most chess players play hundreds of fast games and hardly ever review them. Experience piles up, understanding does not: the same mistakes repeat from game to game.
why.p2: Chess Fundamentals offers another way. It finds the positions in your games where you thought the longest — that is where the game was decided. Work through them yourself, without an engine, write down your thinking and discuss it with a coach. That is how you grow your thinking at the board, not just your game count.

positions.text: Enter your Chess.com or Lichess nickname, and the site finds the moves you thought longest about. They are the best material for analysing on your own.

ask.title: How to ask a question
ask.demoIntro: This is what a finished text looks like. Try it:

find.title: Find a position
find.text: Open “Positions”, enter your Chess.com or Lichess nickname and pick a move you thought about for a long time. Any game under “Games” works too. Press “Ask coach”. You need an account for this.

write.title: Write what you were thinking
write.text: Tap the text field. “Recording” appears above the board: from now on the board writes moves into your text. Describe the moves you considered and what made you doubt.

moves.title: Show lines on the board
moves.text: Drag a piece, or tap it and then tap a square. The move lands in the text where the caret is. Further moves continue the same line.

continue.title: Keep writing
continue.text: Type some more and play again: the new moves land at the caret and continue from the position on the board.

newLine.title: Start another line
newLine.text: “Back to key position” returns the board to the start, and the next moves become a new line. “Undo move” removes the last move. Tap a move in the text to carry on from it.

send.title: Send it
send.text: Press “Send to coach”. If you close the window first, your draft is kept.

tips.keyboard: Playing a move doesn’t open the keyboard. Tap the text when you want to type.
tips.hide: “Hide board” at the top of the window makes room. Your text and moves stay, and “Show board” brings it back.
tips.send: The send button stays at the bottom of the window while you write.

answer.title: How to read an answer
answer.text: Answers appear in “My questions”, in your account menu. Tap a line in the text: the board shows its first move, and the arrows step through it. Try it:
answer.notifications: To hear about answers right away, connect Telegram in your profile.

coach.title: If you are a coach
coach.text: Open “Student questions” in your account menu and press “Reply”. It is the same window: you write an answer the same way as a question, with moves on the board.
